title: What is an ABEND?
text:
An ABEND (Abnormal End) is the term used in IBM Mainframe environments to refer to the abnormal termination of a program, process, or job. It occurs when an application cannot continue execution due to an error, and the system interrupts its operation before it finishes correctly.

An ABEND can be caused by various factors, such as programming errors, incorrect memory accesses, file or database issues, lack of system resources, or instruction execution incidents. When it occurs, the system generates an error code that helps identify the origin of the problem and facilitates its analysis and resolution.

title: How to analyze a system DUMP?
text:
A system dump (SYSMDUMP, SYSUDUMP, or CEEDUMP) is a complete snapshot of the program's state at the time of the ABEND. Analyzing it allows you to identify the exact failing instruction, the corrupted register, the offset, and the responsible module.

Each dump provides a different level of depth:

SYSMDUMP — the most complete (memory, registers, control blocks).

SYSUDUMP — lighter, oriented toward basic debugging.

CEEDUMP — generated by LE (Language Environment), useful for COBOL/PL/I/C.

To analyze it, identify the ABEND, check the PSW, locate the offset of the failed instruction, examine the registers (R0–R15), and map the offset to the program listing. Finally, review storage to detect corrupted data or invalid addresses. This helps determine the root cause of the error.

title: How to interpret an SQLCODE?
text:
SQLCODE is a return code generated by the database manager (usually DB2 in Mainframe environments) after executing an SQL statement. Its function is to indicate whether the operation completed successfully, ended with a warning, or resulted in an error.
The interpretation of an SQLCODE is mainly based on the sign and value of the code:

SQLCODE = 0: The SQL statement executed successfully without any incidents.

SQLCODE positive (> 0): The operation completed, but a warning or special condition occurred that should be reviewed. Although execution continues, a situation may require attention.

SQLCODE negative (< 0): The statement failed and the operation did not complete correctly. In this case, it is necessary to analyze the specific code to identify the cause of the error and apply the corresponding corrective actions.

title: What is the difference between SQLSTATE and SQLCODE?
text:
In DB2 (and standard SQL in general), SQLSTATE and SQLCODE are two different ways of reporting the result of an SQL operation. Both appear in errors, but they do not mean the same thing nor are they used the same way.

SQLCODE is a DB2-specific numeric code that indicates the result of an SQL statement (0 = OK, >0 = warning, <0 = error).

SQLSTATE is a 5-character ANSI standard code that classifies errors portably across databases. SQLCODE is used for detailed technical diagnostics; SQLSTATE is used for compatibility and generic error handling.

title: How does COND work in JCL?
text:
COND is a condition that allows skipping (not executing) a JCL step depending on the return code (RC) of previous steps.
Its function is to prevent running unnecessary or hazardous steps when a prior step fails or returns an unwanted RC.

Fundamental rule of COND:

If the condition is met → the step is NOT executed.

If the condition is NOT met → the step IS executed.

COND controls whether a step should be executed based on the return codes of previous steps. If the condition is met, the step is bypassed. For example, COND=(4,LT) means
It is useful to prevent executing steps when a previous process failed or returned an unexpected RC.

title: What is the difference between JOBLIB and STEPLIB in JCL?
text:
In JCL, both JOBLIB and STEPLIB are used to indicate which libraries (PDS/PDSE) contain the executable programs (load modules) to be used. The difference lies in their scope.

JOBLIB defines the load library for all steps in the job, whereas STEPLIB defines the library only for a specific step.

STEPLIB takes precedence over JOBLIB and is the only one permitted within PROCs. JOBLIB is used for common libraries, and STEPLIB is used for a step's private libraries.

title: What is a parallel batch process?
text:
A parallel batch process is a strategy where a single job is divided into multiple independent subtasks that execute simultaneously, taking advantage of system capacity to reduce execution times and increase throughput.

Instead of processing a file or table sequentially, the work is fragmented, and each fragment is processed in parallel.

Each process handles a part of the input (by range, partition, or source), drastically reducing execution times and enabling more efficient mass loads.
In the end, the results are consolidated into a single output.

title: What is the spool in z/OS?
text:
The spool (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) is a temporary storage area where z/OS saves:

Job output (SYSOUT, messages, listings).

Pending input to be processed (jobs sent to the queue).

That is, the spool acts as an intermediary between programs and output devices (printers, screens, logs).

It allows running jobs without depending on physical devices, centralizes output (SYSOUT, listings, messages), and facilitates review from SDSF. It is essential for batch operation and queue management in JES2/JES3.

title: What is JES2 in z/OS?
text:
JES2 (Job Entry Subsystem 2) is the z/OS component responsible for managing the entry, execution, and output of batch jobs.

Job output (SYSOUT, messages, listings).
It is literally the 'orchestrator' of batch work: it controls queues, the spool, logs, priorities, and resource distribution.

Without JES2, a z/OS system could not execute JCL, manage the spool, or coordinate job execution.

It controls queues, the spool, initiators, logs, and priorities. It is the component that organizes the entire job lifecycle and allows batch to run efficiently and in a controlled manner.
